lines: Notice what just happened. The team said their protocol was correct, and they were right, inside the model their tests actually exercised.
Production simply doesn't run inside that model. It runs inside whatever the real machines and the real network actually do.
So the question worth sitting with isn't what broke. It's which unstated assumption the test suite never challenged in the first place.
Here's the trap worth noticing before you answer. Telling a client a write is acknowledged feels like it settles the matter.
But that sentence is a promise about the future, not a fact about where any byte currently sits.
Ask yourself what actually has to be true on disk, somewhere, for that promise to still be honest a moment later.
answer: The honest answer is yes, on its own, that single dropped message already breaks the promise.
If the only durable copy ever made was the one on the machine that just disappeared, the acknowledgement was already false the moment it was said.
Nothing else needs to go wrong. One silent message is enough.

lines: Resist treating partial synchrony as one vague idea in the middle. The paper actually gives two sharply different shapes for it.
One hides the delay bound from the protocol entirely. The other reveals it, but only after a moment the protocol has no way to detect arriving.
Those aren't the same assumption wearing different words, and a protocol built for one can fail outright under the other.
Here's the correction worth making early. Byzantine isn't just a worse version of a process going silent.
A silent process you can eventually work around by waiting it out or ignoring it. A lying process actively spends effort convincing the others of something false.
That's why outvoting liars costs more spare machines than simply outlasting the silent ones ever did.
Watch the gap between these two promises, because it's smaller than it sounds and people assume it away constantly.
The weaker one only guarantees that trying forever eventually works once. It says nothing at all about any single attempt.
Everything people casually call a reliable connection is really that weaker promise, plus retrying and filtering duplicates, bolted on afterward.
Here's what should actually surprise you. This isn't three different bugs in three different protocols.
It's the exact same handful of lines, run three separate times, failing for three unrelated reasons each time reality supplied a different missing assumption.
That's the real lesson a model buys you: it tells you in advance which of those three failures you're even protected against.
Carry forward the shape of the argument, not just the vocabulary.
A model is a contract a protocol is correct relative to, so ask which contract before trusting any claim of correctness at all.
A lying witness is a different kind of problem than a silent one, never just a worse version of the same problem.
And one small, ordinary-looking protocol just failed three separate ways, each one traced back to a single missing assumption.
Before you answer, think about what those two counters are actually capable of seeing.
A counter can only ever report the thing it was built to count. It cannot report on a fault nobody told it to watch for.
answer: No, and the reason is worth remembering well past this topic.
A reordered pair of messages still counts as nothing dropped. A restart that only lost unflushed memory still counts as nothing crashed, by most definitions a dashboard uses.
A quiet counter is evidence that one particular fault didn't fire. It is never evidence that the underlying model actually held.
